rows: Risk from asbestos arises when fibres are released into the air and inhaled.
Dutyholders for non-domestic premises must identify and manage asbestos-containing materials.
An asbestos register should record the location and condition of known or presumed asbestos-containing materials.
An asbestos management plan should explain how identified risks will be controlled.
Information about asbestos must be shared with workers and contractors who could disturb it.
Work involving asbestos requires a suitable and sufficient risk assessment.
Some higher-risk asbestos work requires a licensed contractor.
Workers liable to disturb asbestos need appropriate information, instruction and training.
Building age or a generic asbestos map does not prove that asbestos is present or damaged at a specific location.
Property-level conclusions require a competent survey, material condition, planned-work and management-record evidence.
Employers must assess risks to workers from noise at work.
Noise exposure should be eliminated or reduced so far as reasonably practicable.
Hearing protection is required where other controls do not reduce exposure enough.
Legal exposure limits must not be exceeded.
Workers need information, instruction and training about noise risks and controls.
Health surveillance is required where there is a risk to hearing.
Noise can also create safety risks by interfering with communication and warning signals.
Control measures should prioritise quieter processes, equipment and engineering controls.
A noisy industry or complaint record does not establish an individual worker's daily exposure.
Exposure conclusions require task duration, measured levels, hearing protection, controls and health-surveillance evidence.
Employers must assess and control health risks from hand-arm vibration.
Regular exposure to vibrating tools can cause hand-arm vibration syndrome and carpal tunnel syndrome.
Alternative processes or lower-vibration equipment should be considered to reduce exposure.
Exposure time should be reduced where elimination is not reasonably practicable.
The daily exposure action value for hand-arm vibration is 2.5 m/s² A(8).
Tools and accessories should be maintained to avoid unnecessary vibration.
Workers need information and training on symptoms, controls and safe tool use.
Health surveillance is required where workers are at risk from hand-arm vibration.
Tool ownership or manufacturer emission data alone does not determine a worker's actual daily exposure.
Risk depends on in-use vibration, trigger time, grip, maintenance, work method and individual susceptibility.
Employers must manage risks arising from electricity at work.
Electrical equipment should be suitable for its environment and intended use.
Equipment and installations must be maintained so they remain safe.
Work on electrical systems should be planned and carried out by competent people.
Electrical supplies should be isolated where reasonably practicable before work begins.
Safe isolation should prevent inadvertent re-energisation during work.
Inspection and testing should be proportionate to equipment type, use and environment.
Damaged or defective electrical equipment should be removed from use or made safe.
An electrical certificate or equipment label does not prove the present condition of every circuit or appliance.
Site conclusions require current inspection, maintenance, loading, environment and competent-person evidence.
